subject: physics
title: Stationary waves
key_idea: Two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions form a stationary wave of fixed nodes and antinodes λ/2 apart. A string fixed at both ends has a first harmonic f₁ = (1 / 2l) √(T / μ).

blocks.text: A stationary wave forms when two waves of the same frequency and similar amplitude travel in opposite directions and superpose. A reflected wave meeting the incoming wave does this.

items.text: A wave travels along a string and reflects from a fixed end.
The incoming and reflected waves pass through each other.
At some points they are always in antiphase and cancel. At others they are always in phase and add.
The result is a fixed pattern of nodes and antinodes. The pattern does not travel.

items.meaning: A point on a stationary wave where the amplitude is always zero.
A point where the amplitude is a maximum.

items: Adjacent nodes, or adjacent antinodes, are λ/2 apart, where λ is the wavelength of the progressive waves forming it.
A node and the next antinode are λ/4 apart.
Between two adjacent nodes all points oscillate in phase, with different amplitudes. Points in neighbouring loops are in antiphase.
If you measure the distance across several loops, divide by the number of loops to find λ/2.
A displacement–position graph at one instant is a sine curve: zero at the nodes, peaks at the antinodes.
At other instants the nodes stay in the same places but the heights of the loops change.
Twice each cycle every point is at zero displacement. Half a period later the loops are at their greatest displacement, with neighbouring loops on opposite sides of the axis.
A graph of amplitude against position shows zero at each node and the maximum at each antinode.

rows: Varies from zero at nodes to maximum at antinodes
Same within a loop; antiphase in neighbouring loops

items: Stationary wave = two waves of equal frequency travelling in opposite directions.
Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart.

sections.heading: Stationary waves on strings and in air

blocks.text: A string fixed at both ends has a node at each end. Only waves that fit this condition last. These are the harmonics.

items: The first harmonic has one loop: length L = λ/2, so f₁ = v / 2L.
The second harmonic has two loops: L = λ, so f₂ = 2f₁.
The nth harmonic has fn = n f₁, with n loops.

blocks.label: Speed of a transverse wave on a string
First harmonic on a string
where: f₁ = frequency of the first harmonic (Hz)

blocks.text: The frequency is higher for a shorter string, a greater tension and a smaller mass per unit length.

diagram.alt: Calculate the first harmonic frequency of a stretched string.
diagram.question: A string of length {l} m has a mass per unit length of {mu} g/m and is stretched with a tension of {T} N. Calculate the frequency of the first harmonic.

items: An open tube has an antinode at each open end. The first harmonic has L = λ/2, so f₁ = v / 2L, and all harmonics are present.
A closed tube has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. The first harmonic has L = λ/4, so f₁ = v / 4L.
A closed tube gives only odd harmonics: f₁, 3f₁, 5f₁, ...
End corrections are ignored.
Microwaves: a transmitter faces a metal reflector. A probe moved between them finds nodes and antinodes λ/2 apart.
Sound: a loudspeaker above a tube of air and a reflecting end give stationary waves of sound.
Fixed ends are nodes; open ends of air columns are antinodes.
A closed tube gives only odd harmonics; an open tube gives all.

checks.q: State two differences between a stationary wave and a progressive wave.
checks.a: In a stationary wave the amplitude varies from zero at nodes to a maximum at antinodes, whereas in a progressive wave it is the same everywhere. A stationary wave does not transfer energy along the wave, whereas a progressive wave does.

checks.q: Adjacent nodes of a stationary microwave pattern are 14 mm apart. Calculate the wavelength and, with c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, the frequency.
A string of length 0.60 m, mass per unit length 2.0 × 10⁻³ kg/m and tension 50 N vibrates in its first harmonic. Calculate its frequency.

items: Describe the lowest frequency as the first harmonic, and the next as the second harmonic.
Give a graphical explanation of how the two waves superpose to produce nodes and antinodes: draw both waves and add them at each position.
Investigate how the frequency of stationary waves on a string depends on length, tension and mass per unit length. Change one variable at a time and keep the others constant.
Plot f against 1/l, f against √T and f against 1/√μ. Each should be a straight line through the origin.
Know stationary-wave experiments with microwaves, stretched strings and air columns.
Explain formation by a graphical method: sketch the two waves at several times to show where the sum is always zero (nodes) and where it reaches a maximum (antinodes).
Find λ from the positions of nodes or antinodes: the distance between adjacent ones is λ/2.
The first harmonic is also called the fundamental mode of vibration.
Determine the speed of sound with a resonance tube: hold a tuning fork of known frequency over a tube in water, and adjust the water level until the loudest sound is heard.
The tube length at the first resonance is λ/4 (end correction ignored), so v = fλ = 4fL.
For better accuracy, find two successive resonances. The difference in tube length is λ/2, which removes the end correction.
